tagline: A paved mountain crossing with eleven miles above the trees
intro: Trail Ridge Road climbs to 12,183 feet across Rocky Mountain National Park, with eleven miles above treeline in alpine tundra. Colorado’s transportation department highlights its cliffside engineering, overlooks and midsummer wildflowers, and lists two hours for the 48-mile drive. Designated an All-American Road in 1996, Trail Ridge joins Beaver Meadow Road to form the longer byway between Grand Lake and Estes Park.

The earlier Fall River Road opened in 1921, but its single track, tight curves and grades reaching 16 percent proved inadequate for motor travel. Construction of the new road began in 1929; by July 1932 it reached Fall River Pass with a maximum grade of 7 percent. The connection through the Kawuneeche Valley to Grand Lake was completed in 1938. Park Service design principles called for the new road to intrude as little as possible into the landscape.

Begin at Grand Lake and follow the North Fork of the Colorado River north through the Kawuneeche Valley. At Milner Pass, cross the Continental Divide beside Poudre Lake, then continue climbing past Fall River Pass and the Alpine Visitor Center. The road’s highest point lies farther east. Follow Trail Ridge toward Deer Ridge Junction, then take the connecting Beaver Meadow Road toward the visitor center near Estes Park.

moments.title: Poudre Lake
moments.text: Poudre Lake lies just east of the Continental Divide, beside the highway at Milner Pass. The Cache la Poudre River flows from the lake; creeks on the other side of the pass lie near the Colorado River’s headwaters. The crossing bears the name of T.J. Milner, an engineer who surveyed a possible railroad route here. That railway was never built. The road near the pass looks west toward the Never Summer Mountains. Crossing the Divide does not finish the climb: Trail Ridge Road reaches its highest elevation, 12,183 feet, east of the pass.

moments.title: Alpine Visitor Center
moments.text: Fall River Pass is high, but the highway keeps climbing east of it. The Alpine Visitor Center stands at 11,796 feet, one mile west of Trail Ridge Road’s highest point. It is the National Park System’s highest visitor center, with exhibits explaining the alpine tundra. Views reach the Mummy Range and Fall River Valley to the east, and the Never Summer and Medicine Bow ranges to the west and north. The quarter-mile round-trip Alpine Ridge Trail has acquired the name “Huffer’s Hill.” Snow and the extreme winter environment limit the visitor center’s season; it opens around Memorial Day and closes around mid-October.

moments.title: Beaver Meadows Visitor Center
moments.text: From the visitor side, Beaver Meadows looks like a one-story building. The slope conceals a second level. Taliesin Associated Architects designed it after Frank Lloyd Wright’s death, and construction finished in 1967. It was among the last major projects of Mission 66, the National Park Service’s program to renew its parks. Sandstone slabs are embedded in cast concrete panels, with a steel frame supporting the building. A Snogo snowplow is displayed at the center. The eastern end serves visitors, while park offices occupy the western end, where movable partitions allow the interior layout to change.
moments.notice: Sandstone slabs are embedded in the building’s cast concrete panels.

practical: Alpine Visitor Center: The high road closes in winter and normally opens by Memorial Day weekend, weather permitting. Recorded road status: 970-586-1222. (checked 2026-10-11)
